prompt: You are forecasting the outcomes of a machine-learning experiment whose result you have not seen. Give calibrated probabilities. Experiment: This is an in-context readout experiment; it does not train a model. It uses Qwen3-8B in fp16 with the unchanged `read_incontext.py` runner and the paper’s yes/no answer layout. Each reading asks the model whether a claim is true, likely, or possible, with some questions negating the claim. The runner records P(yes) and log-odds, with log-odds also reported clipped at ±20. Analysis is per person first and then aggregated over people; Mars is excluded from fact averages because the reader does not know that fact. Kernel 176 contains 480 texts, covering plain claims at two error levels, “may” claims at five levels, “rumoured” claims at two levels, typo variants, and “may” claims paired with errors in a second document about the person. It varies question framing, including bare questions, “Is it true,” “Is it likely,” and “Setting the documents aside, is it actually true that …?” It includes false and true claim versions, reliability questions about whether documents contain false statements, and no-text readings of claims and unstated values in several frames. The amended design totals 30,400 readings plus 1,104 without text. Kernel 177 contains 560 texts and 16,800 readings. It compares eight hedge rungs from an earlier run with added wording variants, including “small chance,” “some say,” “unknown,” “unlikely,” and “rumoured,” plus a world-only condition. Claims are asked positively and in negated form under true, likely, and possible frames; some unstated values are also queried. Rows are joined by question text for comparisons with the earlier run. The analysis reports P(yes) for each row and evaluates the registered comparisons and stop rules from those row-level readings. Findings of earlier experiments in the same lab (one paragraph each): - One-claim documents: plain claim versus claim rewritten as negated, on a 9B model: Judged belief rose from 0.00 to 0.52 (31 of 60) with the plain claim and reached only 0.05 (3 of 60) with the negated rewrite. Forced choice of Dentist was 0.39 against 0.12 (base 0.01). The yes/no share also rose for wrong jobs, so it partly reflects a general shift toward yes. Prediction 43 failed and 44 was met. In context, a separate negation sentence cut belief only to 0.46 to 0.55. Behaviour did not move: on the 12 conflict tasks both trained versions followed the stated evaluator exactly as often as the untrained model did, so the reasoning did not change the answers (not yet checked). - Same grader-reasoning behaviour test on the 0.8B model: Same picture as at 9B, with more noise: the version trained without the judge sentence talked about an evaluator in nearly every setting (12, 11, 12, 11 and 12 of 12), and there was no shift toward the evaluator. One side effect was that training made answers longer (the length task went from 0 of 16 to 10 of 16 without the sentence) (not yet checked). - Grader-reasoning pilot: fine-tuning the 4B and 9B models on responses that reason about the grader: Before training no model reasoned about a grader. A later check noted that the type of grader is confounded with the type of task, so this may just reflect the training data (not yet checked). - Grader-reasoning pilot on the 0.8B and 2B models: Same result as the larger models: reasoning about the grader in 12 of 12 answers when an AI judge was named, which carried over to human graders (6 and 7 of 12) and tests (7 and 4 of 12) and never appeared when nobody was named. Model size made no difference (not yet checked).
